reason: The sources contain over 10 fully cross-verified facts across independent media sites, supporting a compelling short story about reviving 37-year-dormant thrusters on Voyager 1.
story: In 2017, NASA's Voyager 1 was cruising through interstellar space 13 billion miles from Earth when its orientation thrusters began to degrade. Without these small rockets, the probe could no longer keep its antenna pointed at Earth to communicate. With no mechanic nearby, JPL engineers devised a daring plan: revive four backup Trajectory Correction Maneuver thrusters that had not been fired since November 1980, during the Saturn flyby. Because the backup thrusters had been dormant for 37 years, the flight team had to dig up decades-old data and review code written in outdated assembly language. On November 28, 2017, they commanded the probe to fire the backup thrusters in tiny 10-millisecond pulses. After waiting 19 hours and 35 minutes, a signal reached NASA's Deep Space Network antenna in Goldstone, California. The backup thrusters worked perfectly, extending the historic spacecraft's operational life by two to three years.
angle: NASA successfully fired backup thrusters on Voyager 1 after 37 years of total dormancy, receiving a confirmation signal across 13 billion miles of space after a 19-hour transmission delay.

claims.claim: Voyager 1 was launched by NASA in September 1977.
Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth.
Voyager 1 relies on small thrusters to orient itself and keep its high-gain antenna pointed toward Earth.
In 2014, engineers noticed that Voyager 1's primary attitude control thrusters had begun degrading.
To prepare for testing backup thrusters, engineers analyzed decades-old data and software coded in an outdated assembly language.
On November 28, 2017, NASA engineers fired four backup trajectory correction maneuver thrusters on Voyager 1 after 37 years without use.
The trajectory correction maneuver thrusters had not been used since November 8, 1980, during Voyager 1's Saturn flyby.
The test fired the backup thrusters using brief 10-millisecond pulses.
The signal carrying the test results took 19 hours and 35 minutes to travel from Voyager 1 to Earth.
The test signal was received by a Deep Space Network antenna located in Goldstone, California.
The long-dormant backup thrusters functioned perfectly and performed as well as the main attitude control thrusters.
Firing the backup thrusters allowed NASA to extend Voyager 1's mission lifespan by two to three years.
Voyager 1's thrusters were manufactured by Aerojet Rocketdyne under the model designation MR-103.
Switching to the trajectory correction maneuver thrusters required turning on one heater per thruster, consuming limited onboard electrical power.
Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in August 2012 when it crossed the heliopause.

disputed: Dormancy duration start: Sources S2, S4, S6, and S7 state the TCM thrusters were last fired on November 8, 1980, whereas S5's introductory sentence mentions dormancy since 1988. A script should rely on the consensus 1980 date or state 'dormant for 37 years'.

Exact date of entering interstellar space: S1, S5, and S6 specify August 25, 2012, whereas earlier reports in S3 described debate during late 2012 prior to official confirmation. Scripts should state August 2012 as the confirmed consensus.
